The Northern gannet Morus bassanus incubates its single egg for roughly 43 days [ab = roughly 43 days] at a body temperature near 36 °C [T = 36 °C], though ShalWhit1973 noted that this target temperature varies considerably across incubation bouts. Newly hatched chicks are altricial but are quickly brooded, initially weighing approximately 80 grams [Wwb = approximately 80 grams] at emergence. This modest neonatal mass marks the beginning of a rapid growth trajectory that culminates in an asymptotic fledgling mass approaching 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams], a value that exceeds the typical adult body mass of around 3300 grams reported by MontRick1984 for breeding individuals. The nestling phase is energetically demanding, sustained by intensive biparental provisioning of whole fish delivered to the developing chick. Growth rates are steep, reflecting the high-latitude marine environment where the growing season is brief and the energetic demands of thermoregulation are substantial. Parental attendance at the nest is nearly constant during the early weeks, with one adult always present to shield the downy chick from predation and thermal stress, while the other forages at sea. This biparental strategy is essential for achieving the remarkable mass gain observed during the pre-fledging period.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], fledging occurs around 100 days after hatching [tx = around 100 days after hatching]. This extended nestling period is characteristic of large sulids and reflects the time required for the juvenile to develop flight feathers strong enough to support its substantial body mass, which by that stage approaches the plateau of 4000 grams. Post-fledging, the young bird faces a critical period of nutritional independence, during which it must refine its plunge-diving skills without parental provisioning. The fledgling then enters a prolonged juvenile stage, during which it slowly acquires the foraging proficiency and physical condition necessary for successful reproduction. This immature period is distinguished by plumage maturation and gradual development of the skeletal and muscular systems required for sustained flight and deep diving. Few juveniles survive to sexual maturation, as mortality during this dispersal phase is high, driven by inexperience at sea and vulnerability to storms.

Sexual maturity is attained comparatively late for a seabird of this size, with puberty estimated at 300 days after hatching [tp = 300 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. However, the physiological onset of gonadal activity does not immediately translate into breeding; first-year birds rarely hold territory or form pair bonds. Instead, a considerable delay separates puberty from actual nesting, a pattern common among long-lived seabirds. First reproduction is typically deferred until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching], again at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a period that allows the maturing bird to accumulate the body condition, foraging experience, and social dominance necessary to secure a nest site within the dense colony. Breeding site fidelity is high once established, and pairs that successfully rear a chick often remain together for consecutive seasons. This deferred maturity reflects a bet-hedging life-history strategy in which adult survival is prioritized over early reproduction, maximizing lifetime fitness in an unpredictable marine environment.

Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and typically produce only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], a reproductive rate that is exceptionally low among North Atlantic seabirds. This conservative output is consistent with the maximum reproductive rate of one brood annually, and it reflects the extreme energetic investment required to raise a single, large-bodied chick to fledging over the lengthy 100-day nestling period. The long interval between successive clutches, combined with the extended period of parental care, means that a successful breeding pair can raise at most one offspring per season. This strategy imposes a tight demographic constraint: recruitment rates must be very low or adult lifespan must be very long to maintain population stability. The species compensates for its low annual fecundity through elevated adult survival and exceptional longevity. Field records and banding returns indicate that the oldest documented individuals can survive for approximately 37.4 years [am = approximately 37.4 years] at a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], making the Northern gannet one of the longer-lived marine birds in its size class.

Exceptional adult survivorship, with maximum documented lifespans reaching about 37.4 years [am = about 37.4 years], offsets the species' low annual fecundity and is supported by a robust physiological system capable of enduring the costs of repeated deep-diving and long-distance foraging throughout the adult at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] years. The trade-off between current and future reproduction is stark in a species that takes two years to reach first breeding and then produces only one offspring annually. Development begins with a 43-day incubation period (43 days) [ab = 43 days], a duration that represents the first of several life-history milestones, with the 80-gram birth mass (80 grams) [Wwb = 80 grams] standing in stark contrast to the adult mass and underscoring the massive growth required during the nestling period at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This combination of rapid early growth, deferred maturation, extremely low annual fecundity, and exceptional adult survival defines the Northern gannet as a classic K-selected species among seabirds.
